title: Temperature Controls — Shift Leader Walk
description: Take this standing in the kitchen with your thermometer and a cup of ice. You will calibrate, temp real product on your make table, and work through what to do when something is out of temperature. Do everything the way you normally do it.

questions.title: Calibrate your thermometer now, the way you normally do it. Photograph it while you are doing it.
questions.help: Do it exactly how you usually would. Your Area Coach looks at these.

questions.title: Now temp a cold product on your make table. What did it read, in °F?
questions.help: Any cold product — diced ham, sausage, bacon, cheese. Probe into the middle of the product, not against the side of the pan.

questions.title: Photograph the thermometer in that product, with the reading visible.
Which of these cups is the right one to calibrate a thermometer in? Tap it.

hotspots.label: Packed full of ice, water filled in around it
hotspots.why: Ice packed to the rim with water around it is the one that settles at 32 degrees and stays there.

questions.explanation:
The cup packed full of ice with water added. Pack the ice to the top, then fill the gaps with water. The more ice in there, the longer the water holds steady at 32 degrees.

The cups with only a little ice are mostly water sitting at room temperature. That water is not 32 degrees, so anything you check against it is wrong — and you will not know it.

questions.title: A team member stands the thermometer in a cup of ice cubes with no water, waits for the number to stop moving, and says it is calibrated. What is wrong with that?
choices: Nothing — that is how you calibrate a thermometer
There is no water, so nothing is sitting at a known 32 degrees to check the thermometer against
They should have used hot water instead
They should have left it in for a full ten minutes
questions.explanation:
Dry ice cubes have air gaps between them and no steady temperature. It is the ice and water together that settle at 32 degrees.

Without the water there is nothing holding a known temperature, so the reading tells you nothing — and you are now temping product with a thermometer you only think is right.

questions.title: In a properly made ice bath your thermometer reads 36°F. What do you do?
choices: Nothing — 36 is close enough
Adjust or replace it, and tell your manager
Use it anyway and take 4 degrees off every reading in your head
Leave it in the ice longer until it works its way down to 32
questions.explanation:
A thermometer has to be accurate to within 2 degrees. 36 is 4 degrees out, so it fails.

Get it adjusted or swapped and tell your manager — because every temperature you have taken with it until now was wrong by the same amount, and some of those readings were the ones that said product was fine.

questions.title: What is the highest temperature cold product is allowed to be held at?
questions.explanation: 41 degrees or below. Not 42. The make table's air temperature has to hold 41 or less as well, not just the product sitting in it.

questions.title: These pans were just temped. Pepperoni 40°F. Italian sausage 39°F. Diced ham 47°F. Bacon 38°F. Tap the pan that is out of temperature.

hotspots.label: The diced ham at 47°F
hotspots.why: 47 is 6 degrees over the 41 limit. The other three are all at or below 41 and are fine.

questions.explanation:
The diced ham at 47. That is 6 degrees over.

The other three are at or below 41 and are fine — 40 is not 'nearly out', it is in standard. Do not pull product that is passing.

questions.title: You have just found that diced ham at 47°F. What do you do? Pick everything that applies.
choices: Tell your manager straight away
Pull the product off the line now rather than at the end of the shift
Check whether the lid was left open or the pan was overfilled
Top the pan up with fresh cold product to bring the temperature down
Stir it and temp it again in an hour
Nothing — ham is cured, so it is fine
questions.explanation:
Tell your manager — always, every time, before anything else. Then get it off the line and work out why, because the pan next to it is about to do the same thing. The usual causes are a lid left open, a pan overfilled, or too much product pulled out of the cooler at once.

Topping the pan up with fresh product is the one that catches people. It does not cool anything down. It drags the fresh product up to the warm product's temperature, and now you have twice the problem.

questions.title: Your make table itself is not holding temperature — the air inside is reading 48°F. What do you do? Pick everything that applies.
choices: Tell your manager straight away
Record it on the Food Safety Checklist
Contact the service vendor for repair
Check the lids are closed and no wells are open without an insert pan or separator bar
Turn it to the coldest setting and carry on serving
Leave it until tomorrow and see if it sorts itself out
questions.explanation:
Tell your manager first. A make table that is not making temperature is theirs to act on, not something to quietly work around for the rest of the shift.

Then record it, get the vendor called, and check the easy causes while you wait. An open well with nothing in it is a common one — cold air falls straight out of the gap.

questions.title: What is wrong with this make table that would stop it making temperature? Tap it.

hotspots.label: PLACEHOLDER — move this marker onto the open space
hotspots.why: An open space with no pan in it lets the cold air fall straight out, and the rail stops holding temperature.

questions.explanation:
The open space with no pan in it.

Cold air falls straight out of a gap like that, and once it does the line will not keep temperature — not just that space, but the pans either side of it too.

Putting a pan in it is the fix, and an empty pan counts. Every space needs a pan or a separator bar in it, whether you are using that ingredient or not.

questions.title: When do thermometers have to be calibrated?
choices: Every morning, before food prep starts
Once a week
Only when they look wrong
Whenever someone asks to see it
questions.explanation: Every morning, before any food prep. The restaurant also has to keep ice available to do it — bagged ice or filled ice trays count if there is no ice machine.

questions.title: True or false: the goal of calibrating a thermometer is to make it read 32 degrees.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation:
False. It is to check.

We know that a cup of water filled with ice will reach 32 degrees. We need to see whether the thermometer knows that as well.

You are not trying to force the number to 32. You are holding the thermometer up against something you already know is 32 and seeing whether it agrees.
